--- title: "Accessing data & building the book" subtitle: "Reproducible Workflows · Session 2" format: revealjs: footer: A. Stamm · Reproducible Workflows · Session 2 --- # Recap: Session 1 → Session 2 ## Where we are {.inv} Last session you learned the document mechanics; today we fill them with real work. ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: **write**, Quarto documents, structured reports, transparency. - Session 2 (today): **source**, get a real dataset, clean it, **version it with git**, land your analysis inside the **portfolio book**, and pick your Chapter-1 dataset. - Session 3: **publish**, pin the environment (uvr), deepen git (PRs, review), put it at a URL, and finish Chapter 1. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Today's payoff: Chapter 1 (the EDA project) of your portfolio book becomes real. Let's trace the *reproducible* data journey end to end. ::: # The EDA loop & cleaning decisions ## What EDA is for {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Exploratory data analysis (EDA)** is the back-and-forth loop where you learn what the data can tell you: 1. **Get a quick sense**: shapes, types, missingness, ranges. 2. **Look for problems**: wrong types, missing values, inconsistent names/labels, outliers. 3. **Ask & plot**: small targeted plots to answer questions and surface surprises. 4. **Record decisions**: every cleaning choice documented, because a *defensible* choice is a feature. EDA is *iterative*: you circle through 1–3 several times before any formal modelling. The output that survives into a report is the cleaned data **plus the story of your decisions**. ::: ## The environment at a glance {.inv} Your IDE is part of the reproducible loop. In Positron: ::: {.incremental} - **Data pane / variable explorer**: inspect loaded tables and objects without typing. - **Inline plots**: plots render in the IDE as you iterate. - But: the *IDE* is for exploring; the *document* is the record. Anything you discover by clicking must end up as **code in a `.qmd`** to be reproducible. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Rule: **explore by clicking, report by code.** The click is fast; the code is what makes it reproducible. ::: ## One-line summaries: `skimr::skim()` {.inv} A whole data set summarized in one call, the fastest honest "first look": ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Data summary | | | |:------------------------|:--------| |Name |penguins | |Number of rows |344 | |Number of columns |8 | |_______________________ | | |Column type frequency: | | |factor |3 | |numeric |5 | |________________________ | | |Group variables |None | ::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `skim()` shows type, `n_missing`, and mini-distributions per column in one go (here compacted with `|> summary()`). When someone asks "what's in this data?", `skim()` first. ::: ## Cleaning names & counting: `{janitor}` {.inv} Real-world data arrives with messy names and labels. `{janitor}` tidies them: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "species" "island" "bill_length_mm" [4] "bill_depth_mm" "flipper_length_mm" "body_mass_g" [7] "sex" "year" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species n percent Adelie 152 0.4418605 Chinstrap 68 0.1976744 Gentoo 124 0.3604651 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `clean_names()` makes column names *syntactic* (safe to reference); `tabyl()` gives counts with percentages. Both make downstream code far more readable. ::: ## Seeing missingness: `{naniar}` {.inv} Missing data is not an afterthought: it's often the most important thing about a data set. `{naniar}` makes it visible: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where is the penguins data missing, and how much?](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/vis-miss-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `vis_miss()` draws the whole data set as a grid, missing cells in dark. `gg_miss_var()` plots missingness *per column*. Use them to decide *why* data is missing, and whether your analysis needs to care. ::: ## Tying it to Session 1 {.inv} This is the same cleaning conversation you started in the base-R course with `penguins_messy.txt`: ::: {.incremental} - There you fixed wrong **types** (`readr` guessing), separators, and missing values by hand. - Today the **decisions** are the point: `janitor`, `naniar`, `skimr` don't *make* them for you; they *surface* them faster so you can decide well and record why. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The toolkit changed; the habit didn't: **inspect → decide → document.** Every decision you can justify in a sentence is a reproducible decision. ::: ## Your turn: EDA toolkit {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} Run this on the `penguins` data (loaded at the top), or a data frame of your own: 1. `skim(penguins)`: which columns have missing values? How many? 2. `penguins |> clean_names() |> names()`: do names need cleaning? 3. `penguins |> tabyl(species)`: what are the group sizes? 4. `vis_miss(penguins)`: where is the missingness concentrated? 5. Write one sentence: **"I will handle the missingness by … because …"**, that sentence is your reproducible cleaning decision. :::
Going further

~12 min. This is warm-up for Lab 1; stretch by adding a gg_miss_var() plot.

# Sourcing open data ## Open data, anywhere in the world {.inv} A reproducible analysis needs data it can **re-fetch by code**, and open-data portals everywhere provide exactly that: ::: {.incremental} - **France**: [data.gouv.fr](https://www.data.gouv.fr), thousands of public datasets, **license-aware**. - **Your own country**: nearly every government runs an official open-data portal (data.gov… for the US, Canada, UK, Germany, and many more). - **The rule is the same wherever you look**: a dataset you can fetch *programmatically* is a dataset your analysis can re-produce. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The reproducible move: don't *download* a dataset by hand; write code that *sources* it, so the analysis is re-runnable and the provenance (publisher + URL) is in the document. ::: ## `{rdatagouv}`: the French portal from R (an option) {.inv} Because we teach from l'ENSAI, **data.gouv.fr** is a natural default. `{rdatagouv}` (maintained by your instructor) wraps it: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `{rdatagouv}` is an *option, not a requirement*: use it if you pick data.gouv.fr. Any portal you can query with a URL (e.g. `download.file()`) works just as well for reproducibility. ::: ## Fetching any portal by URL {.inv} Whatever portal you choose, the reproducible core is the same: a URL your code downloads: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.incremental} - **`download.file()` is portal-agnostic**: it doesn't care whether the URL points at data.gouv.fr or your home country's portal. - Pair it with a **provenance sentence** (dataset, publisher, URL, license) so a reader can *find* and *trust* the source. - Some portals ship an R/Python client (`{rdatagouv}` here): a convenience, never a requirement. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Live block (≈10 min).** Together: `search_datasets("climat")` *and* browse one non-French portal (e.g. your home country's). Both approaches collapse to the same thing: a URL to download by code. ::: ## Contributing back {.inv} Open data isn't just a source: for many portals it's a community you can help: ::: {.incremental} - **File issues**: wrong metadata, broken links, unclear descriptions: report them. - **Open PRs**: `{rdatagouv}`'s own repo (`github.com/astamm/rdatagouv`) welcomes contributions. - The course explicitly invites this: improving public data is part of the reproducible habit. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Improving the data others (and your future self) rely on is itself a reproducibility act: finding and fixing a broken source helps everyone. ::: ## Lab 1: your dataset {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Lab 1 (≈35 min):** `lab-1-eda-datagouv.qmd`. 1. **Pick a dataset you actually care about**: on data.gouv.fr *or* your own country's official open-data portal (sport, transport, environment, culture…). 2. In a Quarto doc, source it **by code** (no manual download), `{rdatagouv}` for data.gouv, `download.file()` for any portal. 3. Run a quick EDA: `skim()`, `clean_names()`, `tabyl()`, `vis_miss()`. 4. Write 2–3 sentences on your *cleaning decisions*. :::
Lab 1: your dataset

This same dataset becomes Chapter 1 of your portfolio in Lab 2, so choose something you'd be proud to show for the whole term.

# Versioning your data with {pins} ## The (dis)appearing data problem {.inv} Last session you met "the (dis)appearing data": a fetched file can *change* or *vanish* the moment it's off the portal: ::: {.incremental} - A portal updates a dataset: your analysis was based on the **old version**. - A raw URL 404s a year later, and your "reproducible" document can't re-run. - Even locally, `data/my-data.csv` can be overwritten, and git alone doesn't version the *cached* copy well if you don't commit it. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `{pins}` closes that gap: **version your data** the way git versions your code, so a re-render gets the *same* data a reader expects, not whatever is live today. ::: ## `{pins}`: pin data to a versioned board {.inv} `{pins}` stores a data object on a **board** and records **who wrote what, when**: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `pin_write()` snapshots the data and records the **version + hash**; `pin_read()` returns that exact snapshot. Re-render → same data, every time. ::: ## Where the versioned copy lives {.inv} A board is just a folder (or a service), and it's fully inspectable: ::: {.incremental} - `pin_list(board)`: what's been pinned. - `pin_versions(board, "my-dataset")`: every snapshot, with hashes and dates. - `pin_read(board, "my-dataset", version = "…")`: roll back to an older snapshot. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The pinned `pins/` folder is committed alongside your code, so the *exact data* your analysis used is reproducible forever, independent of portal changes or broken URLs. ::: ## Fetch once, pin, analyse {.inv} A reproducible data workflow in three deliberate steps: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Fetch** the open data by URL: provenance recorded. 2. **Pin** it with `pin_write()`: versioned & hashed on a local board. 3. **Analyse from the pinned copy** (`pin_read()`): stable no matter what happens upstream. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Pinning keeps you honest: the *data* you analysed is on record, not just the *code*. Combined with git (code), renv/uv (environment) and a URL (delivery), it completes the durable portfolio you build in Session 3. ::: ## Beyond data: version your models too {.inv} The same "pin what you made" idea extends to the *models* you fit, not just the data: ::: {.incremental} - **[`{vetiver}`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-r/)**: pins a **model** to a board, so the exact trained model is deployed or re-loaded, versioned & reproducible like your data. - It pairs with `pin_write()`/`pin_read()`: you already know the mechanics; vetiver just knows how to save/load a model's metadata too. - Same habit, new object: **data → `{pins}` · model → `{vetiver}` · code → git · environment → renv/uv**. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Saving a trained model by hand usually loses which packages/versions made it. `{vetiver}` records those alongside the model, so it re-runs and re-deploys anywhere. ::: ## R and Python, side by side {.inv} Every reproducibility tool you've met has an equivalent in Python, with the same ideas and the same names: | Role | R | Python | |---|---|---| | **Environment** | [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) / `uv` | [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) / `venv` | | **Data & artifacts** | [`{pins}`](https://pins.rstudio.com) | [`pins`](https://rstudio.github.io/pins-python/) | | **Model versioning/deploy** | [`{vetiver}`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-r/) | [`vetiver`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-python/) | ::: {.callout-desc} Your book is Python-compatible by design: whichever language a chapter uses, the reproducible pipeline (source → pin → version → publish) is the same. ::: # Versioning your code with git ## Git in one habit {.inv} You version your *data* with `{pins}`; you version your *code* with git, one small round at a time: ::: {.term}
$
git status # your compass: where am I?
$
git add # stage the changes you want to keep
$
git commit -m "msg" # snapshot with a note
$
git push # send the snapshot to GitHub ::: ::: {.incremental} - **`usethis::use_git()`** turns the folder into a git repo; the **Positron git pane** is the clickable version of the loop. - **Commit often**: small, descriptive commits beat rare mega-commits; `git status` is your compass. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Version your code the way you just versioned your data. `add → commit → push` is the whole habit; everything else is dress-up. ::: ## A repo + a remote {.inv} Local history is half the story; a **remote** (GitHub) makes it durable and shareable: ::: {.term}
>
usethis::use_git() # make it a git repo
>
usethis::use_github() # create + link the remote, push once ::: ::: {.incremental} - Set up a **GitHub account** first (happygitwithr walks it), then give Positron access. - `usethis::use_github()` creates an `origin` remote and pushes your `main` once, **properly tracked**. - In the Positron git pane, the **push** button sends your commits to GitHub. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} A pushed repo is a backup and a way to share; a local-only repo is one laptop failure from gone. Push early, push often. ::: ## .gitignore: what NOT to commit {.inv} Not everything belongs in history. Tell git to ignore machine-local noise: ::: {.term}
$
cat .gitignore ::: ::: {.incremental} - R: `.Rhistory`, `.RData`, `renv/library/` - Render output: `_book/`, `*_files/` - Editor/OS: `.DS_Store`, `.venv/`, `__pycache__/` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Your `portfolio-book/.gitignore` scaffold already covers these. The rule: **commit source, not output or environment.** Source is what rebuilds everything. ::: ## Branches: keep `main` always-working {.inv} A branch is a second version of history you can work on without touching `main`: ::: {.term}
$
git checkout -b add-cleanup-notes # make + switch to a branch
$
git commit -m "document cleaning" # work there
$
git checkout main && git merge add-cleanup-notes # fold it back ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Mirror how you actually work**: try an idea on a branch, keep it if it works. - **`main` stays always-working**: a broken experiment never reaches the shared history. - In the Positron git pane, the **branch** menu creates and switches branches. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Branches are cheap and disposable: they're how you keep the *main* line always reproducible. **Never push to `main` directly**: in Session 3 you'll decide what merges via a pull request. ::: ## Connect with your instructor {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Mini-lab (~10 min).** Get your book onto GitHub so you can share and get feedback during the gap week: 1. `usethis::use_git()` then `usethis::use_github()` on your portfolio book. 2. Make a real change, commit it, push it (`git add` / `git commit` / `git push`). 3. Create a branch (`git checkout -b eda-chapter-1`) and push it too. :::
Going further

happygitwithr (happygitwithr.com) is the tutorial base: its chapters on git install, connect GitHub, and the commit-push loop cover every step with screenshots. This is how you'll share work and get feedback via GitHub between sessions.

::: {.callout-desc} By the end of today, your book is versioned and remote, ready for Session 3's pull requests and review. ::: # Quarto books ## What a Quarto book is {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} A **book** is many `.qmd` chapters bundled by one config file into a single navigable publication: - `project: type: book` marks the folder as a book. - `_quarto.yml` lists the **chapters** in order and the output options. - Each `.qmd` is a chapter; they can **cross-reference** each other and share figures/tables. - Render once → a whole site with sidebar navigation, TOC, bibliography. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} You already know the document mechanics: a book is the same thing scaled to many files, wired together in `_quarto.yml`. ::: ## Anatomy of `_quarto.yml` {.inv} The book is driven by one small file: ```yaml project: type: book book: title: "My Data Science Portfolio" author: "Your Name" chapters: - index.qmd - chapters/01-EDA.qmd - references.qmd bibliography: references.bib format: html: theme: cosmo ``` ::: {.callout-desc} Add a chapter by appending its path to `chapters:`; list order is book order. ::: ## Make it yours: branding {.inv} The book's look is yours to define. Two files beside `_quarto.yml` control it: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `_brand.yml`: colours & fonts (the zero-CSS on-ramp) ```yaml color: palette: teal: "#2E7D6B" # pick your own accents amber: "#E8A33D" indigo: "#4A5899" ink: "#17251F" paper: "#F1EEE6" primary: teal foreground: ink background: paper ``` ::: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `styles.scss`: structural CSS beyond the palette ```scss /* find selectors via Inspect, then tweak */ .sidebar { width: 300px; } ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} Edit a `"#hex"`, `quarto preview`, look. Match what *you* like, not the course decks. ::: ## Language-agnostic chapters {.inv} A Quarto book happily mixes languages, and so can your portfolio: ::: {.incremental} - Chapter files are just `.qmd`; each chapter can run **R, Python, or both**. - `format: html` and cross-references work identically either way. - That's why your portfolio stays useful as you grow into Python in later courses. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Portfolio-first design:** the scaffold already reserves empty chapters for later instructors (`02-semester-2.qmd`, `03-semester-3.qmd`). Your book is built to grow. ::: ## Lab 2: build your book {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Lab 2 (≈35 min):** `lab-2-portfolio-book.qmd`. 1. **Copy** `common/portfolio-book/` to your own folder (`cp -r … ~/my-portfolio/`). 2. **Render** it: confirm the starter book builds. 3. **Drop your Lab-1 EDA in as Chapter 1** (`chapters/01-EDA.qmd`). 4. Re-render the whole book; check the sidebar and cross-references. :::
Lab 2: your book

By the end of this lab you hold the seed of your portfolio, a book, not just a report. Session 3 puts it under version control and publishes it.

# Finding a great dataset ## Beyond data.gouv.fr: OpenData R packages {.inv} Pick the portal (or package) that gets you to a dataset you *care* about; the reproducibility rule never changes: ::: {.incremental} - **France**: [data.gouv.fr](https://www.data.gouv.fr) via `{rdatagouv}`. - **Your country**: nearly every government runs an official portal (data.gov for the US, Canada, UK, Germany…), fetched by URL. - **R-friendly datasets**: `{tidycensus}` (US Census), `{opendatatoronto}`, `#TidyTuesday` data on GitHub; Kaggle datasets too. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Whatever the source, the bar is the same: you can fetch it **by code** and record its provenance (dataset, publisher, URL, license). If you can download it with one line of code, it's fair game for Chapter 1. ::: ## Choose your dataset before you leave {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Final task of the session (~10 min).** Leave today having chosen your Chapter-1 dataset so Session 3's work block starts fast: 1. **Pick a dataset you actually care about** on data.gouv.fr, your country's portal, or an R-friendly source above. 2. Record its **source by code** (a URL / a package call) and its provenance (publisher, URL, license). 3. Write **one line: the question you want to answer** with it. That question is your IMRAD seed for Chapter 1. :::
Going further

Between now and Session 3 there is a week. If you don't finish, keep refining your dataset and question, and commit it to the eda-chapter-1 branch you made earlier today; your instructor can already comment on it there.

# Writing for an audience ## A report is read, not just rendered {.inv} Your EDA will be read by other humans, instructors, classmates, future employers. Write to *them*: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Structure signals intent**: question, data, cleaning, results, findings. 2. **Captions do the explaining**: a reader should grasp a figure from its caption before reading your prose. 3. **Say what you found *and* what you didn't**: honest limits are credibility. 4. **Keep code in service of the story**: the code shows *how*; the prose says *why it matters*. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The reproducibility narrative: because everything is code and captioned, a stranger re-rendering your `.qmd` both **trusts** and **reproduces** your work. That's the product. ::: ## Preparing work others will extend {.inv} Your chapters are slots other courses will fill. Make that easy: ::: {.incremental} - Use the **same structure** every time (the 5-section recipe). - Give **descriptive labels** to figures/tables (`fig-cap` everywhere). - Keep **setup in one chunk** so new chapters start from a known environment. - Leave placeholder chapters **in place**: they're the roadmap. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Think of the book as a shared, growing artefact, not a one-off. Every convention you follow today lowers the friction for the next instructor who appends a chapter. ::: ## Recap: the full loop {.inv} From data to a readable, reproducible chapter, the whole course in one picture: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Source** open data by code (portal of your choice): provenance recorded. 2. **Explore & clean** (`skimr`/`janitor`/`naniar`): decisions documented. 3. **Report** in a structured chapter: captions, cross-refs, findings. 4. **Assemble** into the book: one navigable portfolio. 5. **Version** your work on git: committed, branched, pushed to GitHub (today). 6. *(Session 3)* **Pin & publish**: uvr/uv (`{pins}` for data), Posit Connect. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Today you've done steps 1–5: your book is sourced, cleaned, assembled, and under version control. Step 6 (Session 3) pins the environment, reviews through a PR, and turns the local book into a shared, durable URL. ::: ## Three moves, one book {.dark auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:88px; top:150px; width:720px; font-size:72px;"} Source, clean, build. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:840px; top:150px; width:150px; height:360px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:1006px; top:150px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:1006px; top:340px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ## Source, clean, build {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} Today your book gained its first real chapter. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="draft" style="left:96px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Source by code]{.h} [Open data fetched by code (any portal) and **pinned** with `{pins}`: provenance (publisher + URL) recorded.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="review" style="left:470px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Clean with evidence]{.h} [`skimr`/`janitor`/`naniar`: decisions documented as *why*, not just *what*, so a stranger can trust them.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:844px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Build Chapter 1]{.h} [Your EDA assembled into the book: captioned, cross-referenced, written for a reader.]{.p} ::: ## Your Chapter 1, committed {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} From a local chapter to a durable, shareable book. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:96px; top:200px; width:800px; height:400px;"} [Build Chapter 1: make it durable next]{.h} [Everything today lives in `01-EDA.qmd` inside your book, **versioned on git** and pushed to GitHub. In Session 3 that chapter becomes published: **uvr/uv** pins its environment and R version (and today's `{pins}` board versions its data), it's reviewed through a **pull request**, then **Posit Connect** gives it a URL. Same book, suddenly a published, reproducible portfolio.]{.p style="font-size:24px; line-height:1.6;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="draft" style="left:944px; top:230px;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="review" style="left:944px; top:290px;"} ::: ## Next time {.dark .finale auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:200px; top:300px; width:880px; font-size:56px; text-align:center;"} Session 3: version it, pin it, publish it. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:470px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:590px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:710px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {style="position:absolute; left:96px; top:600px; width:1024px; font-size:17px; color:rgba(241,238,230,0.62);"} Between sessions: finish `lab-2-portfolio-book.qmd` so your book builds, commit it to GitHub on your `eda-chapter-1` branch, and refine your **Chapter 1** dataset and question. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
